summary: The deck introduces decision trees and explains splitting with a blood-pressure classification example using Gini impurity. It then focuses on Fast-and-Frugal Heuristics and fast-and-frugal trees, highlighting their simplicity, transparency, and clinical use in postoperative ICU admission decisions compared with CCS and ASA-PS scoring. Additional examples include credit card approval, wound infection prediction, and a student performance dataset for analyzing best-case accuracy with different numbers of attributes.

Definition. A fast-and-frugal classification tree such that it: (i) always has an exit after it queries an attribute, (ii) has only a few attributes and (iii) queries each attribute once and does not query multiple attributes together.

Case study: Clinical application of fast-and-frugal trees (FFT): Intensive care
FFT was developed and evaluated for deciding whether a patient should be admitted to the Intensive Care Unit (ICU) or a general nursing ward after surgery.
After surgery, doctors must decide General Nursing Ward or Intensive Care Unit (ICU)
Wrongly sending a high-risk patient to the nursing ward
Increases the risk of complications or death.
May delay critical care.
Wrongly sending a low-risk patient to the ICU
Increases healthcare costs.
Occupies ICU beds unnecessarily.
Hospitals commonly use two approaches:
(a) Charlson Comorbidity Score (CCS): A regression-based risk score.
Calculates risk based on age, existing diseases (diabetes, cancer, kidney disease, etc.)
Produces a numerical risk score.
(b) ASA Physical Status (ASA-PS)
Assigned by an anesthesiologist.
Rates the patient's overall health from 1 to 6.
A large European study analyzed approximately 47,000 surgical patients across 498 hospitals in 28 countries. 73% of patients who died within one week after surgery had never been admitted to the ICU.
Proposed Solution: Fast-and-Frugal Tree
Observe with other ML approaches
Printed FFT on laminated pocket cards. Provide a quick reference
They had memorized the decision tree.
FFT combines objective clinical data already collected in hospitals.
Structured discussions. Improved communication among physicians.
Made it easier to explain decisions to patients.
Real Clinical Example
Patient: Age = 72 years , High CCS
According to the FFT: → ICU admission
However, the doctor did not admit the patient to the ICU.
ICU was already very busy. Although the FFT recommends ICU admission, the patient could be safely managed in the normal ward because enhanced monitoring was available.
FFT is not a rigid rule.
Instead, it serves as a decision support tool.
Doctors can still use their experience when unusual situations arise.
